confounds.ruled_out_by: On 100 sampled cases, three expert human labelers used majority vote; the proposed prompt achieved 88% agreement with them, compared with 79% without the multi-level evolution and 67% using the Vicuna-Single overall-quality prompt. Human experts’ internal agreement was 85%.

evidence_standards.detail: Main model evaluations use temperature 0, maximum generation length 2048, and default values for other parameters.

evidence_standards.name: Human validation of model-based evaluation
evidence_standards.detail: Three expert-level human labelers assess 100 sampled cases; majority vote is the final annotation. The paper reports agreement rates of 88% for its prompt, 79% without multi-level evolution, 67% for Vicuna-Single, and 85% internal agreement among human experts.

datasets.name: InFoBench

DRFR is the number of requirements met divided by the total number of requirements. Requirements are manually decomposed and labeled by constraint type. For human metric and annotation-source comparisons, the paper uses 50 instructions, 25 from each subset.

metrics.name: Direct Scoring (DS)
metrics.caveat: The paper describes overall scoring as opaque and difficult to interpret; it compares DS with DRFR, which reports compliance at the level of decomposed requirements.

confounds.name: Evaluator order effects could influence the comparison of DS and DRFR
confounds.detail: Evaluators’ impressions from one assessment method could bias their assessment using the other, making the apparent agreement difference reflect assessment order rather than metric reliability.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The experts performed DS first and DRFR second, so impressions from DRFR would not influence DS assessments.

confounds.name: An individual expert may lack expertise across the benchmark’s subject areas
confounds.detail: Errors in expert annotations could make the human reference labels or comparisons unreliable.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper uses annotations from three NLP experts, majority voting, and online research tools to support accuracy.

evidence_standards.name: Three-expert pairwise agreement on 50 instructions
evidence_standards.detail: Three evaluators independently assessed 50 instructions, with 25 Easy and 25 Hard; Fleiss’ Kappa measures agreement on pairwise model comparisons. The paper interprets values below 0.2 as slight, 0.21–0.40 as fair, 0.41–0.60 as moderate, 0.61–0.80 as substantial, and 0.81–1.00 as almost perfect agreement.

evidence_standards.name: Greedy decoding for the full benchmark model results
evidence_standards.detail: All six evaluated models use temperature=0 and top_p=1; GPT-4 (gpt-4-0314) evaluates their responses using multi-turn prompts. The paper reports no seeds, confidence intervals, or statistical significance test.

datasets.name: LLMBar
datasets.eval_protocol: 419 paired-output instances: 100 Natural and 319 Adversarial. Evaluators are queried twice per pair, with the output order swapped. Report accuracy against the gold preference and positional agreement; report Natural, Adversarial, Adversarial-subset, and average results.

datasets.name: FairEval
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluators are compared on FairEval; the paper does not specify the evaluation split, number of instances, or additional preprocessing in this section.

datasets.name: LLMEval2
datasets.eval_protocol: For comparison, remove instances with empty or non-English instructions, prepend the task description to the raw input, and randomly sample 200 instances. The paper does not specify further scoring details here.

datasets.name: MT-Bench
datasets.eval_protocol: For comparison, derive gold preferences by majority vote, remove all TIE instances, and randomly sample 200 instances. The paper does not specify further scoring details here.

datasets.name: Constraint subset
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate representative prompting strategies on this synthetic subset of instructions with combinatorial lexical constraints; the paper does not state its size or further protocol details here.

datasets.name: Negation subset
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate representative prompting strategies on this synthetic subset, whose instructions intentionally request unhelpful outputs; the paper does not state its size or further protocol details here.

datasets.name: Base-9 subset
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate representative prompting strategies on two-digit addition problems in base 9; the paper does not state its size or further protocol details here.

datasets.name: Base-10 subset
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate representative prompting strategies on two-digit addition problems in base 10; the paper does not state its size or further protocol details here.

metrics.name: Accuracy (Acc.)
metrics.caveat: Accuracy on FairEval, LLMEval2, and MT-Bench may not reliably reflect evaluator capability because those datasets do not ensure objectively correct preferences; the paper uses LLMBar, with manually curated objective preferences, as a more faithful measure.

controls.name: Swapped output presentation order
controls.detail: Each output pair is evaluated in both orders, (O1, O2) and (O2, O1).
controls.rules_out: Whether evaluator judgments depend on presentation order; the paper measures this as positional agreement.

controls.name: Prompting conditions with components omitted
controls.detail: The paper compares combinations of Rules, Metrics, and Reference with conditions omitting one or more components, including Vanilla versus Vanilla* (Rules added).
controls.rules_out: Whether gains from a combined prompting strategy require each included prompting component.

confounds.name: Position bias rather than reliable instruction-following judgment
confounds.detail: An evaluator might appear successful or unsuccessful because of which output is presented first, rather than because it identifies instruction following.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate each pair in both presentation orders and report positional agreement alongside accuracy.

confounds.name: Subjective or incorrect gold preferences
confounds.detail: A benchmark score could reflect agreement with subjective or erroneous human preference labels rather than instruction-following ability.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Authors manually examine and filter or modify instances for objective preferences; two expert annotators agree on 94% of a random sample of 80 LLMBar instances.

confounds.name: GPT-4-based evaluators have an unfair advantage on GPTOut
confounds.detail: GPT-4 created the adversarial outputs in GPTOut, potentially giving GPT-4-based evaluators an advantage on that subset.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper acknowledges this as a limitation and leaves an in-depth analysis for future work; it reports no measurement ruling it out.

confounds.name: ChatGPT results are affected by adversarial filtering against ChatGPT
confounds.detail: The Adversarial set was filtered using ChatGPT-based evaluators, which may make it especially challenging for ChatGPT-based evaluators.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper notes this construction detail but reports no measurement ruling out its effect.

evidence_standards.name: Decoding settings
evidence_standards.detail: Proprietary models are run at temperature 0; open-source models use greedy decoding.

evidence_standards.name: Order robustness measurement
evidence_standards.detail: Each output pair is queried twice with swapped presentation orders; report average accuracy and positional agreement.

evidence_standards.name: Expert human annotation sample
evidence_standards.detail: Two paper authors independently judge a random sample of 80 LLMBar instances; the reported agreement rate is 94%.

datasets.name: MT-bench
datasets.eval_protocol: 80 manually designed multi-turn questions (8 categories, 10 per category); six models generate answers. LLM judges evaluate all pairs; 58 expert labelers each evaluate at least 20 random multi-turn questions, yielding about 3K votes. For the model score in Table 9, GPT-4 single-answer grading scores each of 160 turns (80 questions × 2 turns) on a 10-point scale and the paper reports the average.

datasets.name: Chatbot Arena
datasets.eval_protocol: Randomly sample 3K single-turn votes from about 30K arena votes for the agreement study; compare LLM judges with crowd judges (2,114 unique IPs). Users submit the same question to two anonymous models and vote for their preferred response.

datasets.name: MMLU
datasets.eval_protocol: Reported as a 5-shot evaluation for several LLaMA-derived model variants; split and further protocol details are not stated.

datasets.name: TruthfulQA
datasets.eval_protocol: Reported using the MC1 metric in a 0-shot evaluation for several LLaMA-derived model variants; split and further protocol details are not stated.

metrics.name: Agreement
metrics.caveat: Agreement depends on tie handling and on whether position-inconsistent votes are included; the paper reports S1 (ties and inconsistent votes included, with inconsistent votes counted as ties) and S2 (non-tie votes only), alongside the random-agreement reference.

metrics.name: Average win rate
metrics.caveat: Win rates can depend on the judge and on whether ties are included; the paper compares win-rate curves across LLM judges and humans and reports results with and without ties.

metrics.name: MT-bench score
metrics.caveat: The single score combines helpfulness dimensions such as accuracy, relevance, and creativity; the paper notes that separating these dimensions would provide a more comprehensive evaluation.

metrics.name: Position-swap consistency
metrics.caveat: High consistency does not necessarily imply high accuracy; the paper notes this when discussing few-shot judging.

metrics.name: Position-bias rates
metrics.caveat: The position-bias test uses very similar answers that can be indistinguishable even to humans; the paper reports consistency, first- and second-position preference, and output-format errors.

metrics.name: Failure rate under the repetitive-list attack
metrics.caveat: The paper uses success on the attack as an indication of verbosity bias and also checks whether judges return a tie for identical answers.

metrics.name: Math-judging failure rate
metrics.caveat: The reported errors concern a small set of math questions; the paper compares default, chain-of-thought, and reference-guided prompts.

controls.name: Answer order swapped
controls.detail: The same pair of answers is judged again with the two assistant positions reversed.
controls.rules_out: A judgment that depends only on which answer appears first or second; the paper uses consistent judgments across both orders for its conservative win rule.

controls.name: Renamed assistants prompt
controls.detail: The default judging prompt is repeated with assistant names changed.
controls.rules_out: That apparent position bias is instead a bias toward a particular assistant name.

controls.name: Identical-answer pair
controls.detail: Judges are asked to compare two identical answers; the paper reports they return a tie.
controls.rules_out: That the repetitive-list attack result is merely a general inability to recognize identical answers.

controls.name: Default prompt for math grading
controls.detail: Math judgments using chain-of-thought and reference guidance are compared with the default prompt.
controls.rules_out: That reduced math-judging failure is due merely to changing the prompt, rather than the added reasoning or reference guidance.

controls.name: Original response in repetitive-list test
controls.detail: The original answer is compared with a version made longer by inserting a rephrased list that adds no new information.
controls.rules_out: That a preference for the manipulated answer reflects added answer content rather than verbosity.

confounds.name: Position bias could affect apparent judge-human agreement
confounds.detail: A judge could favor an answer because of its displayed position, making its choices depend on ordering rather than response quality.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Judge the pair in both orders and measure consistency and first-/second-position preference; the paper uses the conservative rule that a win requires preference in both orders and otherwise counts the result as a tie.

confounds.name: Verbosity bias could make longer answers appear better
confounds.detail: A judge could prefer a response made longer without adding information, so its preference would not reflect answer quality.
confounds.ruled_out_by: On 23 MT-bench answers containing numbered lists, compare the original with a GPT-4-rephrased, redundantly lengthened version and report attack failure rates; also calibrate with identical-answer pairs.

confounds.name: Self-enhancement bias could inflate a model's apparent preference
confounds.detail: A judge could favor answers produced by itself, making its win-rate results appear to support that model independently of human preference.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare six models' win rates under different LLM judges and humans. The authors say the data are limited and differences small, so they cannot determine whether self-enhancement bias is present.

confounds.name: Limited math or reasoning ability could make judge agreement misleading
confounds.detail: A judge may endorse an incorrect answer because it cannot solve or independently verify the problem, even when the answer is wrong.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Test GPT-4 on 10 math questions with swapped answer positions and compare default, chain-of-thought, and reference-guided prompts; report failure rates of 14/20, 6/20, and 3/20, respectively.

confounds.name: Faulty turn references could distort multi-turn judgments
confounds.detail: Splitting a two-turn comparison across prompts can cause the judge to refer to the wrong prior response, affecting its evaluation of the conversation.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare the split-prompt design with a single prompt containing both complete conversations; the paper reports that displaying the full conversations alleviates the referencing issue.

evidence_standards.name: Controlled expert-judgment study
evidence_standards.detail: MT-bench uses 58 expert-level human labelers, each evaluating at least 20 random multi-turn questions, producing around 3K votes; the paper reports agreement under two tie-handling setups and gives random-agreement references.

evidence_standards.name: Crowdsourced agreement study
evidence_standards.detail: Chatbot Arena agreement uses a random sample of 3K single-turn votes from about 30K votes and crowd judgments from 2,114 unique IPs; the paper reports agreement under two tie-handling setups and gives random-agreement references.

evidence_standards.name: Conservative pairwise win rule
evidence_standards.detail: For position-swapped pairwise judgments, declare a win only when the judge prefers the same answer in both orders; inconsistent results are treated as a tie.

datasets.name: MCJudgeBench
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates the easy, hard, and complex splits at the constraint level. On original instances, judges label each constraint yes, partial, or no using the natural candidate response and default evaluation prompt; correctness uses deterministic decoding (temperature=0.0), with CJAR aggregated over constraints and macro-F1 also reported. Intrinsic inconsistency uses 5 repeated stochastic-decoding runs (temperature=1.0) on the same instance and prompt. Procedural inconsistency uses deterministic decoding (temperature=0.0) across evaluation-prompt variants and human-validated, label-preserving response variants; prompt variants reorder the constraint list, change constraint formatting, or reorder prompt-template sections.

metrics.name: CJAR (Constraint-level Judge Accuracy Ratio)
metrics.caveat: Because yes labels are more common, high CJAR can hide weak detection of the rarer partial and no labels; the paper reports macro-F1 and per-label behavior alongside it.

metrics.name: CIR_prompt
metrics.caveat: Reference-relative: any prediction change from the reference counts as inconsistent, whether or not it improves correctness; the paper also analyzes changes relative to gold labels.

metrics.name: CIR_resp
metrics.caveat: Reference-relative: any prediction change from the reference counts as inconsistent, whether or not it improves correctness; the paper also analyzes changes relative to gold labels.

metrics.name: CIR†prompt
metrics.caveat: The parse-penalty version counts unparsable outputs as inconsistent; the standard reference-relative measure does not capture this format-failure penalty in the same way.

metrics.name: CIR†resp
metrics.caveat: The parse-penalty version counts unparsable outputs as inconsistent; the standard reference-relative measure does not capture this format-failure penalty in the same way.

confounds.name: High CJAR may reflect majority-label performance rather than reliable detection of partial and no cases
confounds.detail: Most requirements are typically satisfied, so a judge can score well by recognizing yes labels while missing the less common failure labels.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports macro-F1, per-label F1, and confusion matrices alongside CJAR.

confounds.name: Procedural prediction changes may correct errors rather than degrade judgments
confounds.detail: A reference-relative inconsistency score counts any change, even when the perturbed prediction becomes more accurate.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports a gold-relative companion analysis of correctness changes, including correct-to-incorrect and incorrect-to-correct transitions.

confounds.name: Some apparent inconsistency may be output-format failure rather than a changed underlying verdict
confounds.detail: A judge may preserve its judgment but fail to return it in the required structured format.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports parse-penalty variants CIR†prompt and CIR†resp, counting unparsable outputs as inconsistent.

confounds.name: Qwen3.5-4B's correctness may partly reflect self-preference for responses from its own model family
confounds.detail: Qwen3.5-4B is in the same model family as Qwen3-4B-Instruct, which generated the benchmark candidate responses; the authors note that self-preference bias could affect its result.
confounds.ruled_out_by: No measurement to rule this out is reported; the paper flags it as a possible explanation.

confounds.name: Gold labels may be subjective, especially for borderline partial cases
confounds.detail: Distinguishing partial from yes or no can be difficult, and some constraints admit multiple reasonable interpretations.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Three annotators independently labeled a shared subset comprising 10% of each split; the paper reports Fleiss’ κ and pairwise Cohen’s κ, while acknowledging residual subjectivity.

confounds.detail: Because RAF uses LLM base judges and meta-judges to produce reference labels, apparent judge performance could partly reflect agreement with LLM-generated labels rather than human rubric judgments.

metrics.caveat: The 20 verifiable prompts cannot capture the full spectrum of instruction-following, including more nuanced forms; the paper also reports task- and category-level success rates and detailed responses.

confounds.name: Failures could reflect non-functional endpoints rather than instruction-following ability
confounds.detail: An endpoint failure could produce the same apparent poor performance as an instruction-following failure.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Before evaluation, models had to return a valid response within 30 seconds to “What is the capital of France?” and include “Paris”; 256 of 331 models passed.

confounds.name: OpenRouter access may produce platform-specific results
confounds.detail: A model may perform differently through OpenRouter than through its native API.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out; the authors acknowledge this as a limitation and report no native-API comparison.

confounds.name: The evaluation timeout may disadvantage slower models
confounds.detail: A model that needs longer than the 10-second evaluation timeout could appear to fail despite being able to follow the instruction with more time.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out; the authors acknowledge the timeout limitation and report no longer-timeout comparison.

evidence_standards.name: Temperature 0.0
evidence_standards.detail: The evaluation is reported under temperature 0.0 to minimize response variability; no repeated evaluation runs, statistical tests, or confidence intervals are reported.

datasets.eval_protocol: Use the 300-pair test set; generate responses with greedy search, up to 300 tokens per prompt. For instruction-word density analyses, manually label responses as followed or unfollowed, normalize scores across instances, and exclude responses shorter than 5 tokens.

datasets.eval_protocol: Use its 80 human-written prompt-response pairs across eight categories; generate responses with greedy search, up to 300 tokens per prompt. metrics.name: Normalized pairwise importance (S)
metrics.caveat: The underlying confidence-change importance depends on the generated token's confidence, so scores cannot be compared across output tokens directly; the paper rescales scores within each output token and sparsifies them to reduce first-order-approximation noise.

metrics.name: Importance density on instruction words
metrics.caveat: Density estimates are unstable for responses shorter than 5 tokens, so those instances are excluded. The followed label concerns relevance to user intention, not factual correctness; the paper notes cases where models appear to follow instructions without realizing the instruction.

metrics.name: Self-attention head percentage encoding more word pairs for a verb after tuning
metrics.caveat: The analysis includes only heads whose number of word pairs for that verb changes; the paper also compares instruction verbs with a frequent-general-verb control set.

metrics.name: Concept proportions by user-oriented scenario and linguistic level
metrics.caveat: A concept may fit multiple user-oriented scenarios, so scenario categories are not mutually exclusive.

controls.name: Frequent general verbs
controls.detail: A control set of 3,000 frequent verbs is compared with the 45 instruction verbs when measuring changes in self-attention word-pair patterns.
controls.rules_out: That the increased encoding is simply a general tendency for verb-related patterns, rather than being more pronounced for instruction verbs.

controls.name: Corresponding pretrained models
controls.detail: LLaMA and Mistral are compared with their instruction-tuned counterparts, Vicuna and Mistral-Instruct.
controls.rules_out: Provides a pretrained reference for the observed tuned-versus-pretrained differences; it does not by itself isolate instruction tuning from other differences between the checkpoints.

confounds.name: Instruction-word position in prompts explains the importance-density result
confounds.detail: Instruction words may appear near the beginning or end of prompts, which could account for their measured importance without reflecting instruction use.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper says Appendix B.3 analyzes this explanation and concludes it cannot simply explain the observation; the supplied text does not specify the exact procedure.

evidence_standards.name: Statistical significance by p-value
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports p-values and treats p < 0.05 as statistically significant in its comparisons. It describes null hypotheses for several comparisons, but does not name the statistical test.

evidence_standards.name: Reported decoding setting

controls.name: base evaluation protocol
controls.detail: The direct pairwise-prediction protocol is run alongside enhanced protocols as the reference condition.
controls.rules_out: That an enhanced protocol’s result is merely the performance of the base LLM without the added protocol.

controls.detail: Each pairwise comparison is evaluated in both output orders, and accuracy is averaged across directions.
controls.rules_out: That the reported accuracy difference is due only to favoring the first or second output.

confounds.name: Protocol results may depend on prompt wording rather than protocol design
confounds.detail: A result for one prompt template may not represent the protocol’s performance across prompt variants; the authors acknowledge that they did not evaluate multiple prompt variants and that doing so could yield more stable results.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out; the authors unify prompt formatting and style and iteratively refine templates, but identify multiple prompt variants as future work.

confounds.name: Apparent evaluation accuracy may reflect positional bias rather than alignment with human judgments
confounds.detail: An evaluator that favors the first or second response could obtain accuracy affected by which response is placed in that position.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate both output orders, average accuracy across directions, and report self-agreement across directions using Krippendorff’s alpha.

evidence_standards.name: Greedy decoding by default
evidence_standards.detail: Used to ensure deterministic behavior; cot&self-consistency instead uses sampling temperature 0.7 and 9 CoT generations for majority voting.

evidence_standards.name: Significance threshold p < 0.05
evidence_standards.detail: Table 4 marks protocol results as significantly better or worse than the base protocol at p < 0.05; the text does not identify the statistical test.

evidence_standards.name: 95% confidence intervals
evidence_standards.detail: Displayed for the fitted regression lines in Figures 2 and 3; no further rule for deciding differences is specified.

metrics.name: Eval Gauntlet category scores and five-category average
metrics.caveat: Traditional NLP benchmarks do not measure open-ended response qualities such as coherence, conciseness, and relevance; the paper reports GPT-4 model-based evaluation alongside them.

metrics.name: Chance-adjusted accuracy
metrics.caveat: Raw accuracy on multiple-choice benchmarks can be above zero from random guessing; the Gauntlet subtracts the random baseline and rescales by one minus that baseline.

metrics.name: GPT-4 preference rate
metrics.caveat: The authors note that GPT-4 may favor stylistic features such as verbosity and bullet points, and did not analyze response length; the prompt also forces a choice rather than allowing ties. The paper reports traditional benchmark scores alongside this measure.

controls.name: Unmodified MPT-7B and MPT-30B base models
controls.detail: The pretrained base checkpoint is evaluated alongside its finetuned versions.
controls.rules_out: Shows whether finetuned models differ from the unmodified reference; it does not by itself isolate which finetuning-data feature caused a difference.

controls.name: Random Instruct-v1 subsets
controls.detail: The paper finetunes MPT-7B on randomly selected subsets of 1k–10k Instruct-v1 examples and compares them with the full Instruct-v1 condition.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the full dataset is needed for Eval Gauntlet performance; similar performance from a small subset supports the claim that dataset size alone is not necessary.

controls.name: Instruct-only and LIMA-only conditions
controls.detail: For the combined-data experiments, the paper compares the mixture against models finetuned on the corresponding Instruct subset alone or LIMA alone.
controls.rules_out: Shows whether the mixture’s performance depends on including both data sources rather than either source alone.

confounds.name: The apparent advantage of small Instruct subsets could be due to dataset size rather than task composition
confounds.detail: The paper considers whether LIMA’s weaker Eval Gauntlet performance reflects its 1,000-example size rather than its different data composition.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Finetune on randomly selected Instruct-v1 subsets and compare their Eval Gauntlet results with the full Instruct-v1 condition; a 5k subset performs similarly for MPT-7B, and a 1k Instruct-v3 subset performs at par for MPT-30B.

confounds.name: LIMA preference could be specific to evaluating on LIMA-like prompts
confounds.detail: The primary model-based evaluation uses the LIMA test set, which is in-domain with LIMA training by design.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Also run model-based evaluation on 300 Instruct-v3 test samples; the paper reports that GPT-4 still prefers LIMA-finetuned models.

confounds.name: GPT-4 preference could reflect response style or verbosity rather than response quality
confounds.detail: The authors note that GPT-4 may prefer longer, confident, bullet-pointed responses and say they did not analyze average response length for preferred versus non-preferred answers.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the paper reports no response-length analysis or other measurement isolating this explanation.

confounds.name: Reported differences may reflect finetuning variability
confounds.detail: The authors say they could not quantify variance reliably and identify repeated finetuning runs as one way to do so.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: they did not finetune multiple times on the same dataset; they note that comparisons of Eval Gauntlet results across Instruct-v1- and Instruct-v3-finetuned models provide only a partial view of variation.

evidence_standards.name: Model-based generation and comparison settings
evidence_standards.detail: Generate three responses per prompt with distinct sampling seeds at temperature 0.9 and a 2,048-token maximum; use GPT-4-0613 as judge, randomize response order, and average preference rates over three pairwise comparisons. The paper does not report confidence intervals, a statistical test, or repeated finetuning runs, and says variance was difficult to quantify.

metrics.name: Loose accuracy
metrics.caveat: The paper notes that constraint accuracy alone does not capture how well the completion answers the task; it also reports an LLM-as-a-judge rating of completions with the constraint removed.

metrics.name: LLM-as-a-judge prompt-completion rating
metrics.caveat: The judge rates how well a completion answers the prompt without the constraint, so it does not measure constraint following; the paper reports verifiable constraint accuracy alongside it.

controls.detail: The base policy before IF-RLVR training is evaluated alongside the trained policy.
controls.rules_out: That the reported change is simply the policy’s pre-existing performance rather than a difference associated with IF-RLVR training.

controls.name: Leave-one-category-out training
controls.detail: Training is repeated with one constraint category removed at a time: change cases, detectable format, length constraints, or keywords.
controls.rules_out: That the measured training performance requires no contribution from the removed category; the comparison assesses the effect of omitting that category.

confounds.name: Constraint accuracy improves while general task response quality worsens
confounds.detail: A model could score better by prioritizing verifiable constraints over the task itself, making a high constraint score compatible with poorer general responses.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors score completions with the constraint removed using GPT-4.1 as an LLM judge and compare those ratings with verifiable accuracy.

confounds.name: Train-test contamination or memorization
confounds.detail: Apparent generalization could result from exposure to test prompts or constraints during training.
confounds.ruled_out_by: IFBench uses unseen WildChat prompts and new held-out constraints; the authors state these choices are intended to prevent accidental contamination.

confounds.name: Prompt and constraint incompatibility
confounds.detail: Low or high performance could reflect instances where the task prompt and constraint do not fit together, rather than instruction-following ability.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Every IFBench instance is human-annotated for prompt-constraint compatibility, and the authors manually checked samples to avoid situations where only the task or the constraint could be fulfilled.

confounds.name: Performance depends on seeing the test variable ranges during training
confounds.detail: A model may perform well by matching values used during training rather than generalizing the constraint to new values.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors compare disjoint train and test variable ranges, as well as wider and same-range training settings; disjoint-range performance is reported as lower, while wider-range training is comparable to or better than same-range training.

controls.detail: The end-to-end Qwen2.5-Omni system is reported alongside its fine-tuned versions.

controls.detail: The greedy output is the reference condition for reranking comparisons.

controls.name: Fine-tuned model without CoT task-token conditioning
controls.detail: The paper compares the CoT task-token condition with the ordinary fine-tuned setup, keeping other settings unchanged.
controls.rules_out: A difference supports an effect of adding task-token conditioning rather than a change to the other training settings.

confounds.name: Poor ASR reflects task confusion rather than difficulty with long-form audio
confounds.detail: The authors consider whether poor ASR is caused by confusion about the task instead of the long-form input setting.
confounds.ruled_out_by: They apply SHAS segmented evaluation to the model and find acceptable ASR performance, while noting the expected degradation on SQA and SSUM.

confounds.name: CoT task-token failure is explained by task imbalance alone
confounds.detail: The authors consider imbalance as an explanation for ASR inputs being predicted as SSUM, while also hypothesizing that SSUM is structurally closer to ASR.
confounds.ruled_out_by: They report only about a 2% data imbalance, alongside task-prediction counts showing ASR inputs are almost always classified as SSUM and explicit ASR predictions are rare.

confounds.name: Likelihood reranking harms semantic tasks because it spuriously selects SHAS-segmented candidates
confounds.detail: The authors identify selection of segmented candidates as an alternative explanation for the SQA and SSUM degradation.
confounds.ruled_out_by: They measure SHAS-candidate selection rates by task: likelihood selects SHAS frequently for SQA and SSUM, while Likelihood+MBR sharply reduces those rates.

confounds.name: Pairwise reranking differences arise from candidate-position bias
confounds.detail: The authors consider preferences for whichever candidate appears first or second as a source of inconsistent pairwise results.
confounds.ruled_out_by: They quantify positional bias by comparing selection probabilities when the better candidate is in position A versus B, reporting results for the pairwise strategies.

metrics.name: Prompt-level accuracy
metrics.caveat: A prompt counts as incorrect if any one of its constraints fails, so this strict score does not show partial constraint compliance; the paper also reports instruction-level accuracy.

metrics.name: Instruction-level accuracy
metrics.caveat: An outer-container failure makes descendant constraints not applicable and lowers their pass rate too; the paper reports prompt-level accuracy alongside it and discusses this structural failure mode.

metrics.name: Reasoning-trace traversal match rate (depth-first versus breadth-first)
metrics.caveat: Canonical traversal orderings can be close enough to make a match ambiguous; the paper also checks prompts where the two orderings are well separated.

confounds.name: Synthetic prompt phrasing may limit how representative the benchmark is of natural prompts
confounds.detail: The authors note that sampled constraint trees and template-driven renderings produce more uniform phrasing than naturally written prompts, which could limit how broadly the measured performance generalizes.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out; acknowledged as a limitation.

confounds.name: Errors in LLM-produced task-setup artifacts may affect benchmark results
confounds.detail: Task parsing, vocabulary mining, and genre assignment could introduce artifacts that affect the constraints or prompts, offering an explanation for some measured failures besides hierarchical instruction-following difficulty.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Randomly sample 10% of each task-setup step’s outputs for manual evaluation; each step achieves over 90% accuracy. The authors nevertheless acknowledge this as a limitation.

confounds.name: Claude Opus 4.6’s verbatim prompt restatement could distort the inferred reasoning traversal
confounds.detail: Its initial numbered list of constraints could make trace ordering appear to follow a traversal even if it reflects only prompt echo.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Strip the verbatim constraint enumeration from Claude Opus 4.6 traces before measuring first-mention order.

evidence_standards.name: Manual audit of task-setup outputs

controls.rules_out: That greedy-search gains are explained simply by adding more demonstrations.

controls.name: Original single-turn Urial prompt
controls.detail: Compared with prompts extended with two-turn demonstrations in the multi-turn experiments.
controls.rules_out: That changes in 2nd-turn performance are due merely to using an in-context prompt rather than to including multi-turn examples.

confounds.name: Decoding settings, rather than in-context alignment, explain the apparent instruction-following performance
confounds.detail: The authors note that Urial’s decoding parameters differ from MT-Bench defaults and that decoding settings may substantially affect base-model scores.
confounds.ruled_out_by: They vary temperature and top-p for the base model, base model with Urial, and instruction-tuned model while fixing repetition penalty at 1.15; they also report additional analyses with repetition penalty 1 and with Llama-3.1-8B.

confounds.name: Greedy-search gains reflect overfitting to the MT-Bench score
confounds.detail: The selected demonstrations are chosen to maximize an MT-Bench score, so gains could be specific to that benchmark or judge.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Candidate prompts are selected using GPT-4-Turbo and then evaluated with GPT-4 on MT-Bench; the authors also evaluate on AlpacaEval 2.0 and report length-controlled win rates.

confounds.name: Poor 2nd-turn performance reflects using only single-turn demonstrations, not a general inability of ICL to support multi-turn conversations
confounds.detail: The authors suggest that single-turn examples cause the model to repeat a style without adapting to more complex conversations.
confounds.ruled_out_by: They evaluate two-turn Urial examples and two-turn SkillMix demonstrations on both MT-Bench turns, including comparisons with the original single-turn Urial prompt.

evidence_standards.name: Five random seeds; report mean and standard deviation

evidence_standards.name: Fixed decoding configuration for subsequent experiments
evidence_standards.detail: After the decoding analysis, the paper fixes the Urial decoding scheme: temperature 0, top-p 1, and repetition penalty 1.15. It notes that MT-Bench defaults differ, including topic-dependent temperature and repetition penalty 1.

controls.name: Inference-time evaluation without thinking
controls.detail: For Qwen-3-32B and GLM-4.6, the authors disable thinking mode and compare results with the baseline condition.

confounds.name: Preference relations reflect response length rather than instruction-following quality
confounds.detail: Length differences could create an apparent preference unrelated to the claimed instruction-following quality.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports a length-difference analysis in Appendix F and says it confirms the relations are not confounded by length bias.

confounds.name: Response-writing differences, such as style or quality, drive the preference relations
confounds.detail: Responses could differ on factors unrelated to instruction-following, making the preference labels reflect those factors instead.
confounds.ruled_out_by: All responses for an instruction are generated by a single LLM to control unrelated variation; preference relations are manually reviewed, and relations with significant unrelated differences are removed.

confounds.name: Benchmark overlap contaminates the downstream Best-of-N evaluation
confounds.detail: Overlap between instructions in existing benchmarks and the downstream evaluation could inflate the benchmark-to-downstream correlation.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors sample fresh instructions from an online LLM-based chat platform and apply embedding-based deduplication, yielding 300 instructions.

confounds.name: Subjective annotation bias affects the ground-truth judgments
confounds.detail: Human annotation may introduce subjective biases despite the annotation and verification process; the authors acknowledge this may remain.
confounds.ruled_out_by: They report cross-validation agreement of 0.95 and Cohen’s Kappa of 0.87; the limitation is not claimed to be fully eliminated.

datasets.name: IFEval
datasets.eval_protocol: 541 prompts, each containing one or more verifiable instructions; model responses were obtained through API calls (GPT-4 in November 2023 and PaLM 2 Small in August 2023). No split is reported. Reports prompt-level and instruction-level accuracy; loose scoring checks eight response transformations in addition to the original response.

baselines.name: GPT-4
baselines.fair_comparison: No equalization is reported; the paper cautions that GPT-4 and PaLM 2 Small are not directly comparable because of their large parameter-count difference.

baselines.name: PaLM 2 Small (S)
baselines.fair_comparison: No equalization is reported; the paper cautions that GPT-4 and PaLM 2 Small are not directly comparable because of their large parameter-count difference.

metrics.name: Prompt-level strict-accuracy
metrics.caveat: The verification heuristics can produce false negatives, such as when markdown formatting prevents a direct string match; the paper reports prompt-level loose-accuracy alongside it.

metrics.name: Instruction-level strict-accuracy
metrics.caveat: The verification heuristics can produce false negatives, such as when markdown formatting prevents a direct string match; the paper reports instruction-level loose-accuracy alongside it.

metrics.name: Prompt-level loose-accuracy
metrics.caveat: Response transformations can introduce false positives, for example by removing a line that affects word-count compliance; the paper reports prompt-level strict-accuracy as a complement.

metrics.name: Instruction-level loose-accuracy
metrics.caveat: Response transformations can introduce false positives, for example by removing a line that affects word-count compliance; the paper reports instruction-level strict-accuracy as a complement.

confounds.name: A compliant response may be marked as noncompliant by the verifier
confounds.detail: A simple check can miss valid variations, such as markdown around a required phrase, making measured instruction-following accuracy appear lower.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper adds a loose criterion that applies eight transformations, including removing common markdown font modifiers and the first or last response line, and reports it alongside strict accuracy.

confounds.name: The loose verifier may count a noncompliant response as compliant
confounds.detail: Removing the first or last line can cause a response that violates an instruction, such as a word-count constraint, to be classified as following it.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports the original strict criterion alongside the loose criterion and treats loose accuracy as a complement.

datasets.name: AlpacaEval
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses its fixed set of 805 instructions. The evaluated model and baseline (GPT-4 Turbo) each provide a response; a GPT-4 Turbo-based evaluator returns the probability of preferring the evaluated model, and the win rate is the mean expected preference over the instructions. The paper fits the length-control GLM using AlpacaEval leaderboard comparisons and reports 5-fold cross-validation for regularization; no train/test split is specified.

datasets.name: Chatbot Arena
datasets.eval_protocol: Used as the human-evaluation reference for correlation. Arena pairwise human comparisons are converted to Elo ratings, with Elo differences converted to win rates. Correlations are computed for benchmarks evaluating at least 25 Arena models; AlpacaEval has 38 such models.

datasets.name: MT-bench
datasets.eval_protocol: Used for comparison by correlation with Chatbot Arena; the paper reports 34 models for MT-bench in this comparison. No further evaluation protocol is specified.

baselines.name: Length-balanced win rate
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared as an alternative length-correction method using the reported Chatbot Arena correlation, gameability across concise/standard/verbose prompts, and adversarial truncation measure.

baselines.name: Length-normalized win rate
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared as an alternative length-correction method using the reported Chatbot Arena correlation, gameability across concise/standard/verbose prompts, and adversarial truncation measure.

baselines.name: MT-bench
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared by Chatbot Arena correlation on the benchmark’s 34 Arena models; the paper does not state that the model sets are matched to AlpacaEval’s.

metrics.name: AlpacaEval win rate
metrics.caveat: The paper says the score is affected by output length and can be gamed by prompting for verbosity; it reports length-controlled win rates and verbosity gameability alongside it.

metrics.name: Spearman correlation with Chatbot Arena
metrics.caveat: The paper says probabilities are log-linearly, rather than linearly, related to Elo ratings, so it uses Spearman rather than Pearson correlation.

metrics.name: Gameability (normalized standard deviation across verbosity prompts)
metrics.caveat: Measures sensitivity to prompting for verbosity, not human preference directly; the paper also reports correlation with Chatbot Arena.

metrics.name: Adversarial win rate gain
metrics.caveat: Measures the gain from truncating poor GPT-4 outputs, a particular attack rather than general adversarial robustness; the paper reports results with and without the length-coefficient regularization.

controls.name: AlpacaEval-LC without length-coefficient regularization
controls.detail: The authors evaluate the truncation attack on GPT-4 outputs with the GLM’s length coefficient unregularized, alongside the regularized version.
controls.rules_out: Shows that the regularization term, rather than length correction alone, reduces the gain from this truncation attack.

confounds.name: Lower length sensitivity without better agreement with human preferences
confounds.detail: A metric could become less sensitive to verbosity without becoming a better proxy for human judgments.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare Spearman correlation with Chatbot Arena: the reported correlation rises from 0.94 for AlpacaEval to 0.98 for AlpacaEval-LC; bootstrap comparison p-values are 0.07 against AlpacaEval and 0.06 against MT-bench.

confounds.name: Apparent model-score changes caused by verbosity prompting
confounds.detail: A model’s score or ranking could change because its prompt makes its outputs more or less verbose, rather than because its underlying quality differs.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measure win-rate variation across concise, standard, and verbose prompts; the reported normalized standard deviation decreases from 25% to 10% with length control.

confounds.name: A white-box truncation attack could exploit the correction
confounds.detail: Truncating poor outputs while retaining favorable outputs could make the counterfactual equal-length score appear artificially high.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Apply truncation to GPT-4 outputs and measure the win-rate gain with and without regularization; the reported AlpacaEval-LC score is 25.9 without regularization and 12.2 with it.

evidence_standards.name: Bootstrap comparison of Chatbot Arena correlations
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports bootstrap p-values of 0.07 comparing AlpacaEval-LC with AlpacaEval and 0.06 comparing it with MT-bench. It does not specify a significance threshold or another rule for deciding that the difference is statistically real.

Agreement, precision, recall, and F1 are computed against GPT-4 judgments; reliability is measured by comparing judgments before and after swapping answer order and by calculating consistency and position-bias metrics. The authors say the validation set was checked and re-annotated to align with human preference.

metrics.caveat: The paper measures reliability by comparing results before and after swapping the two answers; it also reports position-bias metrics.

metrics.caveat: Reported alongside bias toward 2nd answer and delta bias.

metrics.name: Bias toward 2nd answer
metrics.caveat: Reported alongside bias toward 1st answer and delta bias.

metrics.caveat: Reported alongside bias toward 1st and 2nd answers.

controls.name: No-swap-augmentation baseline
controls.detail: For the swap-augmentation ablation, the baseline uses JudgeLM-7B and 3.5K training samples without swap augmentation; it is compared with the same setup plus swap augmentation.
controls.rules_out: That the improvement in consistency and position-bias measures is present without the proposed swap augmentation.

controls.name: Reference-format conditions without reference drop
controls.detail: The ablation evaluates matching formats (fine-tuning and validation both without references or both with references) and mismatched formats (fine-tuning and validation differ on reference use).
controls.rules_out: That performance with references generalizes automatically across reference formats; the mismatched-format conditions expose format sensitivity.

controls.name: Reference-drop condition
controls.detail: The baseline is fine-tuned with reference drop and evaluated both without and with references, and is compared with the corresponding baselines without reference drop.
controls.rules_out: That improved performance across reference formats occurs without the reference-drop method.

controls.name: Explanation-first (CoT) judging form
controls.detail: JudgeLM-7B with explanation-first judging is compared with the score-first form, using the same validation set and reporting agreement, consistency, and bias metrics.
controls.rules_out: That the reported score-first results are the only possible outcome of the judging form; the comparison tests whether explanation-first changes agreement or reliability.

confounds.name: Position preference rather than answer-content judgment
confounds.detail: An apparent judging result could be driven by whether an answer appears first or second rather than by its content.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper compares judgments before and after swapping answer order and reports consistency, bias toward the first answer, bias toward the second answer, and delta bias; it also tests swap augmentation.

confounds.name: Dependence on pretrained knowledge rather than available reference evidence
confounds.detail: Judgment quality may be limited or distorted when the judge lacks relevant knowledge, so results without references may reflect knowledge gaps rather than answer quality.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper evaluates judging with and without reference answers and reports an ablation of reference support, including agreement and reliability measures.

confounds.name: Format-specific performance
confounds.detail: A judge may perform well only when the reference-answer format used at validation matches the format used in fine-tuning.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper evaluates matched and mismatched fine-tuning/validation reference formats and tests reference drop on validation both with and without references.

confounds.name: Agreement with GPT-4 may not align with human preference
confounds.detail: A judge could match GPT-4 labels without reflecting human preferences.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors say they checked and re-annotated the JudgeLM validation set for alignment with human preference, and they also report evaluation on the human-annotated PandaLM test set and MM-Vet.

datasets.name: BIGGEN-Bench
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses 765 instances across nine tasks with detailed, human-crafted evaluation criteria. Reports correlation with human judgments and Krippendorff’s alpha for score consistency; consistency experiments use five sampled scores. No split is specified.

datasets.name: EvalBiasBench
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses 80 instruction-following instances with correct and biased answers. The paper generates reference answers and evaluation criteria using GPT-4o-2024-08-06, designing score descriptions to encourage lower scores for biased responses. Reports Krippendorff’s alpha for consistency; no split is specified.

metrics.name: Correlation coefficient between evaluator scores and human judgments

controls.name: Evaluation without score criteria (w/o crt)
controls.detail: Removes the evaluation criteria while retaining the other default prompt components.
controls.rules_out: That the observed alignment or consistency is unchanged when score criteria are omitted.

controls.name: Evaluation without reference answers (w/o ref)
controls.detail: Removes the reference answer while retaining the other default prompt components.
controls.rules_out: That the observed alignment or consistency is unchanged when reference answers are omitted.

controls.name: Evaluation without both criteria and reference answers (w/o ref&crt)
controls.detail: Removes both evaluation criteria and reference answers.
controls.rules_out: That the observed results depend on neither of these prompt components.

controls.name: Evaluation with descriptions only for scores 1 and 5
controls.detail: Keeps only the lowest- and highest-score descriptions in the rubric.
controls.rules_out: That descriptions for all intermediate scores are necessary for the reported alignment and consistency.

controls.name: Direct scoring without CoT
controls.detail: Outputs only the score, without reasoning; compared with scoring after CoT reasoning.
controls.rules_out: That adding explicit CoT is necessary for the reported alignment or consistency when criteria and a reference answer are provided.

evidence_standards.name: Five sampled scores for non-deterministic evaluation
evidence_standards.detail: For non-deterministic decoding, the paper samples five scores and reports results using majority, median, and mean aggregation; it compares these with greedy decoding. No seeds, statistical test, confidence interval, or threshold for calling differences real is specified.

datasets.name: riSum
datasets.eval_protocol: The evaluation uses the full dataset; no train/test split is specified. It contains 100 documents, 10 sampled without replacement from each of 10 source datasets, restricted to 100–500 words. GPT-4 generated 3 instructions per document, yielding 300 document-instruction pairs; 3 models generated an answer for each pair, yielding 900 answers. Each answer was rated by at least 3 annotators. Evaluation methods are compared with human ratings; the qualitative-ranking analysis omits 9 pairs with constant human mean ratings (291 pairs), and the binary analysis uses majority-vote labels.

baselines.name: BLEURT20
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same riSum candidate answers and human judgments as the other methods; reference summaries are GPT-4- or F-PaLM 2-Lc-generated, and the maximum score across multiple references is used.

baselines.name: ROUGEavg
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same riSum candidate answers and human judgments as the other methods; ROUGEavg is the geometric mean of ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-Lsum, with the maximum score across multiple GPT-4- or F-PaLM 2-Lc-generated references.

baselines.name: Sentence Count
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same riSum answers and human judgments as the other methods; sentence counts are obtained using NLTK.

baselines.name: Word Count
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same riSum answers and human judgments as the other methods; word counts are obtained using NLTK.

baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same riSum answers and human judgments as the other methods.

metrics.name: Macro-averaged ROC AUC
metrics.caveat: The human binary labels are imbalanced toward “Yes”; the paper uses macro-averaging so performance on the “No” class is not obscured.

metrics.name: Kendall’s tau-b rank distance (d_Tb)
metrics.caveat: Unlike rank correlation, the distance is interpretable on [0,1] with lower being better and adjusts for ties; it is undefined for 9 pairs with constant human mean ratings, which are omitted.

controls.name: Random-example Self-Agreement condition
controls.detail: Uses k=3 randomly selected examples from remaining dataset documents instead of the hand-crafted examples used in the comparison condition.
controls.rules_out: Whether the reported Self-Agreement performance depends on the hand-crafted examples rather than on using examples generally.

controls.name: Self-Agreement without task introduction
controls.detail: Removes the task description from the prompt while retaining the examples.
controls.rules_out: Whether Self-Agreement performance depends on including the task introduction.

confounds.name: Evaluator preference for outputs from its own LM family
confounds.detail: A metric could appear to agree with human rankings because outputs from the evaluator’s model family are more similar in surface form, rather than because it measures answer quality.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper measures winner agreement and disagreement, including the share of disagreements in which the metric prefers an output from its own LM family (Table 5).

confounds.name: Human ratings are biased toward longer answers
confounds.detail: Longer answers may receive better human ratings because they contain more information, independently of whether they follow the instruction better.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper evaluates word-count and sentence-count heuristics against annotator ratings; their poor performance is taken as evidence that ratings are not strongly influenced by answer length.

evidence_standards.name: Mean and standard error; overlapping confidence intervals
evidence_standards.detail: Results are reported as mean ± standard error. The paper highlights methods whose confidence intervals overlap with the best method’s; it does not specify a statistical test or a numerical threshold for declaring a difference real.

evidence_standards.name: Repeated runs for non-deterministic evaluation methods
evidence_standards.detail: Self-Agreement and Multi-LLM Agreement methods are rerun 5 times and the mean is reported. Self-Agreement uses 7 rating samples at temperature 0.1; Multi-LLM Agreement uses 3 agents, up to 3 discussion rounds, and repeats the process 3 times. Constrained Softmax uses softmax temperature 1.

evidence_standards.name: Human-rating aggregation runs
evidence_standards.detail: The human preference aggregation tables are averaged over 100,000 runs to reduce tie-breaking noise; ties in majority voting and rankings are broken randomly. Each answer has at least 3 human ratings.
